### Computing the schedule For the second frame, the first CPU stage cannot start at its arrival time of 1 ms: that resource remains occupied until 8 ms. After preparation ends at 16 ms, copying ends at 20 ms, but the GPU is still processing the first frame until 32 ms. The second frame therefore runs on the GPU from 32 to 52 ms and leaves postprocessing at 55 ms. Its 54 ms response time consists of 35 ms of service and 19 ms of waiting. All entries in this table are milliseconds measured from the first arrival: | Arrival | CPU | Copy | GPU | Command | |---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 0 | 8 | 12 | 32 | 35 | | 1 | 16 | 20 | 52 | 55 | | 2 | 24 | 28 | 72 | 75 | Each resource handles one frame at a time in arrival order. The CPU, copy engine, GPU and command stage are assumed independent, with unlimited buffers between stages. A stage can start when its input has arrived **and** its previous frame has finished. With arrival time $a_i$, service duration $s_j$, start time $B_{i,j}$ and finish time $C_{i,j}$: $$ \begin{aligned} C_{i,-1}&=a_i,\qquad C_{-1,j}=0,\\ B_{i,j}&=\max(C_{i,j-1},C_{i-1,j}),\\ C_{i,j}&=B_{i,j}+s_j. \end{aligned} $$ The two arguments of the maximum represent different dependencies: the same frame at the preceding stage, and the preceding frame at the same stage. There is no clock forcing every stage to take 20 ms. This differs from the synchronous digital circuit in the MIT diagram: the diagram explains overlap and frame identity, while the recurrence below schedules variable-duration stages as soon as both dependencies permit them to run. ~~~python from math import isfinite def stage_timeline(arrivals, services): arrivals, services = list(arrivals), list(services) if (not services or any(not isfinite(x) or x <= 0 for x in services) or any(not isfinite(x) or x < 0 for x in arrivals) or any(a > b for a, b in zip(arrivals, arrivals[1:]))): raise ValueError("sorted nonnegative arrivals and positive service times required") available = [0] * len(services) finishes = [] for arrival in arrivals: ready = arrival row = [] for j, service in enumerate(services): start = max(ready, available[j]) ready = start + service available[j] = ready row.append(ready) finishes.append(row) return finishes arrivals = [0, 1, 2] serial = stage_timeline(arrivals, [35]) pipelined = stage_timeline(arrivals, [8, 4, 20, 3]) assert serial == [[35], [70], [105]] assert pipelined == [[8, 12, 32, 35], [16, 20, 52, 55], [24, 28, 72, 75]] serial_latency = [row[-1] - a for a, row in zip(arrivals, serial)] pipeline_latency = [row[-1] - a for a, row in zip(arrivals, pipelined)] assert serial_latency == [35, 69, 103] assert pipeline_latency == [35, 54, 73] print("serial:", serial_latency, "pipeline:", pipeline_latency) ~~~ This is a deterministic teaching calculation, not a CUDA benchmark. Sharing a CPU between preparation and command dispatch would introduce another resource dependency. A copy engine that cannot overlap with the kernel would also invalidate the four-independent-resource assumption. Actual stage times and permitted overlap must come from the implementation; the recurrence cannot establish them. ### Rejecting work that will miss its deadline Consider the serial implementation again. When the second frame arrives at 1 ms, 34 ms of the first frame's service remain. Accepting the new frame would produce a result at 70 ms, beyond its absolute deadline of $1+50=51$ ms. In this fixed-service example the server can detect that failure before doing the work. A simple admission rule accepts a frame only when its predicted finish is no later than its arrival plus 50 ms. Rejection leaves the already accepted work unchanged: ~~~python def admit_serial(arrivals, service, budget): # Validate the same arrival/service assumptions as stage_timeline. stage_timeline(arrivals, [service]) if not isfinite(budget) or budget < 0: raise ValueError("nonnegative finite deadline budget required") available = 0 accepted, rejected = [], [] for i, arrival in enumerate(arrivals): predicted_finish = max(arrival, available) + service if predicted_finish > arrival + budget: rejected.append(i) else: available = predicted_finish accepted.append((i, predicted_finish)) return accepted, rejected accepted, rejected = admit_serial(arrivals, service=35, budget=50) assert accepted == [(0, 35)] assert rejected == [1, 2] print("accepted:", accepted, "rejected:", rejected) ~~~ The accepted responses now have a mean latency of 35 ms instead of 69 ms. That does not mean all three frames were handled better: two received no model result. Over the repeating 120 ms period, total input remains 25 frames/s but on-time model completions are only $1/0.12\approx8.33$ frames/s. Without rejection the serial server also produces just one on-time result per period, although it spends time completing the other two after their deadlines. For the factory, rejection must therefore trigger a defined action, such as routing the part to manual inspection. That action has its own latency and capacity limit; neither is modeled by this program. Report accepted, late, rejected and fallback-handled work against the original input count. A latency percentile calculated only over successful responses hides the rejected population. The rule also relies on knowing the remaining service time. An estimate from past measurements is not a hard upper bound. Variable image sizes, other workloads and thermal throttling can make an admitted frame late. Deadline-aware admission and bounded queues are discussed in [Google SRE, Handling Overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/); here they are applied only to the fully specified deterministic example. ### Mean response time and frames in flight Count every frame from arrival until completion, including both queueing and processing. In one 120 ms period of the original serial example, the first frame contributes 35 frame-ms to that count, the second 69, and the third 103. The system is empty before the next period starts. Consequently its time-averaged population is $$ \overline N=\frac{35+69+103}{120}=1.725. $$ The mean response time is 69 ms and the input rate is $3/120=0.025$ frames/ms. Their product gives the same answer: $$ \overline N=\lambda\overline W =0.025\cdot69=1.725. $$ This is Little's law, applied to a period with no unfinished work at its boundaries. The area under the frame-count curve is also the sum of the three response times: each frame contributes one unit of population for its entire residence. Repeating the identical period makes this finite accounting an exact long-run average. For general traffic, the relation requires consistent measurement boundaries and well-defined long-run averages; no Poisson or exponential assumption is needed. See [Harvard Model Serving, Little's Law](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/13_model_serving/13_model_serving.html). ~~~python period_ms = 120 rate_per_ms = len(arrivals) / period_ms for latencies, expected_population in [ (serial_latency, 1.725), (pipeline_latency, 1.35) ]: mean_latency_ms = sum(latencies) / len(latencies) area_population = sum(latencies) / period_ms assert abs(area_population - rate_per_ms * mean_latency_ms) < 1e-12 assert abs(area_population - expected_population) < 1e-12 print("mean latency:", mean_latency_ms, "mean population:", area_population) ~~~ For the four-stage pipeline, the mean response time is 54 ms and the mean population is 1.35. Both systems still reach a population of three after the third arrival. An average below two does not imply that two buffers suffice, and it says nothing about the 50 ms deadline. The population includes waiting frames; it is not the GPU batch size. After admission control, the accepted population has its own rate, $1/120$ frames/ms, and mean residence time of 35 ms. Multiplying the original input rate by the accepted-only mean mixes different populations. Little's law does not repair a mismatched measurement. Queueing distributions, capacity planning and tail-latency models continue in [[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/14 Inference и оптимизация/58c Queueing и capacity planning|Queueing and capacity planning]]. ## Данные, алгоритм и оборудование
